newsitem.title: USA: U.S. retail sales surge, markets dive on rate fears.
newsitem.headline: U.S. retail sales surge, markets dive on rate fears.

text.p: Retail sales gained strongly in February after the steepest surge during January in nearly a year, the Commerce Department said Thursday, pushing the economy ahead briskly as the year began.

The report of a 0.8 percent rise in February sales to a seasonally adjusted $213.18 billion, after a steeply revised 1.5 percent January jump, sent financial markets into a tailspin on fears it boosted chances of an interest-rate hike to head off inflation.

The department more than doubled its original estimate of an 0.6 percent January sales increase. As a result, January's sales gain was the strongest for any month since February last year, when it shot up 1.9 percent.
"This economy seems to be going full steam with only little sign of a tempering in growth later this year," said economist Anthony Chan of Banc One Investment Advisors Corp. in Columbus, Ohio.

Federal Reserve Vice-Chairwoman Alice Rivlin, speaking briefly to reporters little more than a week before a key central bank session on interest-rate policy, said she was uncertain whether the economy was growing at too fast a clip.

Another policy-maker who will participate in the Federal Open Market Committee meeting on March 25, Chicago Fed President Michael Moskow, told a meeting of the Industrial Relations Research Association that the central bank must always be prepared to act preemptively against inflation if that is necessary to preserve economic expansion.
Recalling that the Fed did tighten in 1994 to foil budding inflation pressures, Moskow said, "I think it was absolutely the right thing."
On the New York Stock Exchange, fear of rising rates helped trigger a plunge of more than 160 points in the Dow Jones industrial average.
Prices for the bellwether 30-year bond fell nearly a full point while the yield, which moves in the opposite direction to prices, kicked up to 6.96 percent. It was the highest yield this year.

The report of booming retail business was just one indicator that strong job growth was pushing consumer confidence to levels apt to fan policy-makers' concern about the potential for escalating wage and price rises.

Separately, the Labour Department said new applications for jobless benefits dropped to 307,000 in the week ended March 8 from 312,000 in the prior week. A four-week moving average that smooths out weekly fluctuations was down to 310,250 applicants from 310,500 in the week ended March 1.
"We could be looking at another 3 percent or more GDP (gross domestic product) growth rate this quarter," said Philadelphia-based economist Joel Naroff of First Union Corp.
Total national output measured by GDP expanded at a brisk 3.9 percent annual rate in the final three months last year.

Most analysts had expected GDP growth to slow to about a 2.5 percent rate in the first quarter -- closer to the Federal Reserve's preferred pace of between 2 percent and 2.25 percent -- but strong consumer spending was forcing upward revisions.
"This expansion has gotten its second, or third, or maybe even its fourth wind," Naroff said.
The economy completed its sixth year of unbroken growth since the last recession in 1990-91. With consumer spending fuelling two-thirds of national activity, it appeared set to plough steadily ahead.

Consumer willingness to spend, often on credit, has regulators concerned. A warning went out to banks Thursday following an American Bankers Association report that credit-card delinquencies hit record levels late last year.

Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig told banks to tighten their standards for issuing credit cards, adding: "The role of the regulator is to take action before potential problems become real problems."

In the fourth quarter of 1996, the bankers' group said, late payments jumped to 3.72 percent of credit card accounts, the highest rate since it began tracking delinquencies in 1980 and up from 3.34 percent in the same period in 1995.
Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich said Thursday that consumers were going "gangbusters" on spending in February and prospects for economic growth were "very strong" in the first quarter.
Fed policy-makers will meet on March 25 to assess whether interest rates should be raised for the first time in nearly two years to keep inflation in check.
Analysts said odds for an increase in March were rising, though it was not a certainty.

"I'm not sure it's going to be in March but almost certainly in May," said Banc One's Chan, referring to the May 20 meeting of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, the next one after the March 25 session.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has warned that the central bank might move pre-emptively, by raising rates, to dampen the risk that inflation could threaten the economy's expansion.
